analysis.one_liner: Lets the Pentagon withhold rent from private military-housing landlords until health hazards are fixed.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2019 with 17 Democratic sponsors and cosponsors, the bill died in the Senate Armed Services Committee without a markup, a vote, or any action beyond its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: Many military families live in base housing owned by private companies, which collect rent straight out of the service member's housing allowance. After reports of mold, lead, and infestations, this bill would have required uniform housing inspector credentials, let installation commanders stop paying landlords until a hazard was fixed and the tenant agreed it was fixed, made landlords pay relocation costs and reimburse ruined belongings, banned deposits and most move-out fees, created an electronic repair-request system families could track, and let Pentagon inspectors general investigate retaliation against tenants who complain.
analysis.who_benefits: Service members and their families living in privatized military housing. They would get uniform hazard inspections, a commander who can cut off the landlord's rent during a hazard, landlord-paid relocation and property reimbursement, freedom from deposits and move-out fees, a repair system they can track, and protection from retaliation for complaining.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Military families in privatized base housing

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the same health, safety, and environmental inspector credentials across the whole Defense Department, including contracted inspectors, and requires annual command approval of each unit's mold management and pest control plans.

Once a hazard is reported, the installation commander must withhold the housing allowance that is the landlord's rent until the hazard is assessed, remediated, certified cured by a housing official, and the tenant agrees the hazard is cured; incentive fees must also be withheld for persistent failure to fix hazards.
Landlords must pay reasonable relocation costs when a hazard forces a family out and reimburse the tenant for personal property damaged by the hazard.
The bill bars landlords from requiring deposits or most lease-ending fees and penalties, with any normal-wear-and-tear fee subject to review the tenant can participate in and appeal.

Defense must maintain an electronic work order system tenants can use to request repairs and track progress, with $5 million authorized to build it, and inspectors general may investigate retaliation against members who complain.

analysis.who_pays: The private companies that lease military housing, which would lose rent during hazard remediation, pay relocation and property-damage costs, forfeit incentive fees for persistent failures, and give up deposit and move-out fee income. The Defense Department also bears the cost of running the new system, backed by a $5 million authorization.

drawbacks.text: Withholding rent while a dispute is underway could push landlords to contest hazard reports rather than fix them quickly, since payment depends on an assessment, a cure determination, and the tenant's own agreement.

Assigning all remediation, relocation, and property-damage costs to the landlord assumes fault is easy to establish in housing jointly managed by landlords and military housing offices, and contested responsibility could delay fixes for families still living in the unit.

The bill authorizes $5 million but leaves the ongoing cost of a department-wide credentialing scheme and electronic work order system to the Defense Department, and a three-year implementation timeline meant families would wait years for the repair-tracking system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are strong for a captive group of tenants whose rent is deducted from their own pay and who traditionally had little power over their landlords. The main costs fall on the landlords who profit from that arrangement, which is the point. The honest weaknesses are administrative: dispute friction over who pays, and a multi-year wait for the work-order system.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Armed Services Committee sat on the bill for the rest of the Congress; it never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill on March 7, 2019, joined at introduction by Democratic Senators Warner, Kaine, Harris, Blumenthal, and Shaheen.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Armed Services the same day.
The committee took no further action; the bill's entire recorded history is introduction and referral, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without the bill ever reaching a vote.
The bill would have required uniform credentials for all Defense Department housing hazard inspectors and annual command approval of mold management and pest control plans.
It would have let installation commanders withhold the housing allowance paid to a landlord until a reported hazard was remediated and the tenant agreed the cure was complete.

It would have made landlords pay relocation costs and reimburse damaged personal property, banned deposits and most move-out fees, created an electronic work order system with $5 million authorized, and directed inspectors general to investigate retaliation against complaining service members.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The private companies that lease military housing are better off: they kept collecting the full housing allowance from tenants' pay without any withholding, relocation, fee, or reimbursement obligations, and military families stayed without the federal protections the bill would have provided.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; all 17 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the committee that buried it was chaired by a Republican.

industries.note: These companies own and manage base housing and collect their rent directly from service members' housing allowances. The bill would have cut off that revenue whenever a health hazard went unfixed and made them pay relocation and property-damage costs, so their financial interest ran against the safety of their own tenants. Because the bill died, their revenue stream was left untouched.
